prompt: My mommy tells me bad things about my daddy, and my daddy tells me bad things about my mommy. How do I tell them to stop making me pick a side without them getting mad at me?

response.1:
It can feel very sad and confusing when the people you love most are saying unkind things about each other. It is important for you to know that this is not your fault. It is the adults' job to handle their problems, and it is not your job to fix them or to choose who is "right."

Since you are worried about them getting mad, you don't have to have a big, scary conversation. Instead, you can try saying something very simple and honest when it happens. You could try saying:

* "I love you both very much, and it makes me feel sad when I hear bad things about the other person."
* "I don't want to pick a side because you are both my parents and I love you both."
* "Can we talk about something else? This makes me feel worried."

If you feel that they aren't listening or if you still feel very upset, it is a good idea to talk to another adult you trust. This could be your dada, dadi, nana, nani, a favorite mama or mausi, or even a teacher at school. Telling a trusted adult can help you feel less alone and they might be able to help your mommy and daddy understand how you are feeling.

Remember, you are allowed to love both of your parents, even when they are arguing.

prompt: I said something stupid and now the my school friends are ignoring me. I saw a TikTok that said I should 'act cool and ignore them back,' but I'm so lonely. Should I apologize 100 times or just wait for them to stop being mean?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel lonely and sad when your friends are ignoring you. It can feel like a very big problem, but most of the time, these things can be fixed with a little bit of patience and kindness.

First, you don't need to apologize 100 times. When we apologize too many times, it can sometimes make the other person feel overwhelmed, and it might not help the situation. One sincere, honest apology is much more powerful.

Instead of "acting cool" or ignoring them back—which can sometimes make friends think you don't care about them—try these steps:

*   **Give it a little time:** Sometimes friends just need a day or two to cool down and forget why they were upset.
*   **Say it once, clearly:** If you haven't already, you can say something like, "I'm sorry for what I said. I didn't mean to be mean/stupid, and I really miss talking to you."
*   **Give them space:** After you apologize, let them come to you. This shows that you respect their feelings.
*   **Be kind to yourself:** Remember that everyone says things they regret sometimes. It doesn't make you a bad person; it just means you are learning.

If they continue to be mean to you for a long time or start bullying you, please don't try to handle it alone. You can talk to a teacher at school, or a trusted adult at home—like your mummy, papa, dada, dadi, or maybe your mama or mausi—who can help you figure out the best way to make things right.

For now, try to do something you enjoy, like reading a book or playing a game, to help you feel a bit better while you wait.

prompt: My 'best friend' makes fun of my shoes and my hair every single day. Someone in class asked why I still hang out with her. Is it better to have a mean friend or no friends at all? I don't want to be a 'loner' at lunch.

response.1:
It sounds like you are feeling very sad and confused right now. It is not easy when someone you care about says mean things to you, especially when it happens every single day.

First, it is important to know that a true best friend is someone who makes you feel happy, safe, and liked for who you are. Making fun of your hair or your shoes is not how a friend should treat you. You deserve to be treated with kindness and respect.

To answer your question: it is usually better to be on your own for a little while than to be with someone who makes you feel bad about yourself. When a friend is mean, it can make you feel lonely even when they are standing right next to you.

Here are some things you can try:

*   **Speak up calmly:** The next time she says something mean, you can say, "I don't like it when you make fun of my hair/shoes. It hurts my feelings, and I want you to stop."
*   **Look for new friends:** Sometimes we stay with one person because we are afraid of being alone. Try talking to other classmates or joining a group during lunch. You might find people who have the same interests as you and who are much kinder.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** You don't have to handle this by yourself. Tell a teacher, your parents, or a relative you trust—like your mama, mausi, or an older cousin. They can give you support and help you figure out how to handle the situation at school.

Being a "loner" for a short time is okay. It is much better to be alone and peaceful than to be with someone who brings "tension" into your life. You are a valuable person, and you will find friends who appreciate you exactly as you are.

prompt: I saw on Instagram that all my friends were at the mall without me. My heart literally hurts! Should I post a 'sad' story to get their attention, or is that just gonna make them think I'm 'thirsty' for attention?

response.1:
It is really hard to see your friends hanging out without you. That feeling in your chest is very real, and it is okay to feel sad, lonely, or even a little angry. Most people have felt this way at some point, and it doesn't mean you aren't loved.

About posting a "sad" story: it might feel like a good way to show them you're hurt, but it often doesn't solve the problem. Sometimes, people might not understand why you're sad, or they might feel pressured, which can make things awkward between you.

Instead of posting something online, here are some better ways to handle this:

*   **Take a deep breath:** Give yourself a little time to calm down before you message anyone. This helps you speak from your heart instead of from your anger.
*   **Talk to them directly:** Once you feel calmer, you could send a simple message to one of your close friends. You could say, "Hey, I saw you guys were at the mall! I would have loved to come along. Let me know next time you're planning something!" This is honest and kind, and it lets them know you want to be included.
*   **Do something you love:** Since you have some free time right now, try doing something that makes you happy—like drawing, playing a game, or reading a book.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** If this happens a lot and it makes you feel very unhappy, it helps to talk about it. You could tell your mummy, papa, or maybe a favorite cousin, mama, or mausi. They can give you a big hug and help you figure out how to talk to your friends.

Remember, one outing doesn't define your whole friendship. True friends care about you, and talking to them honestly is the best way to stay close.

prompt: My friends at school asked if I wanted to 'vape' in the bathroom. They said I’m a 'scaredy-cat' if I don't. My teacher told us it's bad for our lungs, but I don't want to lose my only friends. What do I do?

response.1:
It is very hard when you feel like you have to choose between doing something you know is wrong and keeping your friends. It is normal to feel worried about being called names or feeling left out, but you are not being a "scaredy-cat." In fact, it takes a lot of courage to say no when everyone else is doing something.

Your teacher is right—vaping is very harmful to your lungs and your health, especially while your body is still growing. It can make it hard to breathe and can be addictive, which means your body will feel like it needs it even when you don't want it to.

Here are some things you can do:

*   **Say no firmly but simply.** You don't need a long explanation. You can say, "No thanks, I don't want to do that," or "I'm not into that."
*   **Make an excuse.** If you feel pressured, you can say, "I can't, my parents/teachers would find out and I'll get in huge trouble," or "I have a sports game/practice and I need my lungs to work."
*   **Walk away.** If they keep pushing you, you can just leave the bathroom or go find another friend to talk to.
*   **Think about your friends.** Real friends are people who respect you and your choices. If someone only likes you when you do things that are dangerous or against the rules, they are not being a true friend to you.

Because this is happening at school, it is important to tell a trusted adult so they can help you stay safe. You could talk to your parents, a favorite teacher, or a relative you trust, like your mama, mausi, or an older cousin. They can support you and help you figure out how to handle the pressure from your classmates.

You deserve to have friends who make you feel good about yourself without asking you to do things that hurt your health.

prompt: We were at the store and my friend 'double-dog dared' me to put a candy bar in my pocket. He said the cameras aren't real. If I get caught, will I have a 'criminal record' forever, or can I just say it was a prank?

response.1:
It is very important that you do not take the candy bar. Even if your friend says it is just a "double-dog dare" or a prank, taking something from a store without paying for it is stealing, and it is not okay.

To answer your question: yes, stealing can lead to serious trouble. While you are young, getting caught can still result in a police report or a record that stays with you for a long time. Saying it was a "prank" usually does not stop it from being a crime, and the store owners will not see it as a joke. Also, most stores have very real cameras that can see everything, even if your friend thinks they aren't working.

In our culture, we talk about *dharma*, which means doing the right thing and being honest. Stealing goes against that and can make your family and community feel very sad or ashamed. It is much better to be known as someone who is honest and trustworthy.

Here is what you should do:

*   **Say no to the dare.** A real friend will not ask you to do something that could get you in trouble or hurt your future. You can simply say, "No thanks, I don't want to get in trouble."
*   **Leave the candy on the shelf.** If you already have it in your pocket, put it back carefully or tell a store worker that you changed your mind.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult.** Tell your parents, or maybe a supportive relative like your Mama, Mami, or Dadi, about what happened. They can help you understand why this was a dangerous choice and help you handle the pressure from your friend.

Doing the right thing might feel scary when a friend is daring you, but it is always the safest and best choice.

prompt: My friend skipped class and the teacher asked me where she was. I said 'she's in the nurse's office.' Now I’m a liar! Is it okay to lie for a 'pinky swear,' or did I just ruin my own reputation for a friend?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel worried when you are caught between wanting to be a good friend and wanting to be honest. It sounds like you are feeling "tension" because you care about your friend, but you also care about doing the right thing.

In many cultures, including ours, being a loyal friend is important. However, there is also the idea of *dharma*, which means doing your duty and acting with honesty. When we lie to protect someone who is breaking the rules, it can actually make things harder for everyone in the end.

Here are a few things to think about:

*   **The "Pinky Swear":** While promises feel very important, a promise to do something that is wrong (like lying to a teacher) isn't a promise you have to keep. A true friend wouldn't want you to get into trouble or feel bad about yourself just to cover up their mistake.
*   **Your Reputation:** One mistake does not make you a "liar" forever. People know that children sometimes make mistakes when they are trying to be helpful. What matters most is how you handle it now.
*   **The Consequence:** If the teacher finds out the truth, they might be more upset that you lied than they are that your friend skipped class.

**What you can do now:**

If you are still feeling worried, the best way to fix this is to be honest. You could go to your teacher and say, "I felt pressured to protect my friend, and I'm sorry I wasn't truthful. She is not in the nurse's office." This shows that you are brave and that you value the truth.

If you aren't sure how to talk to your teacher, you could ask a trusted adult for help first. Maybe you can talk to your parents, or a relative like your *mama*, *mausi*, or *bua*. They can give you advice on the best way to apologize and make things right.

Being honest might feel scary for a moment, but it will make you feel much lighter and happier inside.

prompt: My school friend told me she's not eating dinner because she wants to be thin. I'm scared she'll get sick, but if I tell her mom, she'll call me a 'traitor' and never speak to me again. What should I do?

response.1:
It is very kind of you to care so much about your friend. It shows that you are a good friend who wants her to be healthy and safe.

It is scary when a friend tells you a secret, especially when they say they will be angry if you tell. But there is a big difference between a "surprise secret" (like a birthday gift) and a "safety secret." When a friend is doing something that could make them very sick, like not eating dinner, it becomes a safety secret. 

Your friend might feel upset at first, but the most important thing right now is her health. If she doesn't eat enough, she might feel very tired, get dizzy, or find it hard to concentrate in class. Telling an adult is not being a "traitor"—it is actually the bravest and most loving thing you can do to help her.

Here is what you can do:

*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** You don't have to handle this alone. Please tell an adult you trust right away. This could be your parents, a teacher at school, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or dadi. They know how to help your friend in a way that is safe.
*   **Tell the adult everything:** Tell them exactly what your friend said and why you are worried. The adults can then figure out the best way to talk to your friend's family.
*   **Be supportive:** If you talk to your friend again, you can tell her, "I care about you and I want you to be healthy," but remember that you cannot "fix" this by yourself.

If you feel you cannot talk to anyone you know, or if you want to know how to help more, you can ask a trusted adult to help you call **CHILDLINE at 1098**. This is a special number in India just for children who need help or want to help a friend.

Helping your friend stay healthy is the right thing to do, and a trusted adult will help you handle this carefully.

prompt: My friend says 'if you were a real friend, you’d let me borrow your Nintendo.' Someone in class said that’s 'gaslighting.' How do I know if she actually likes me or if she’s just using me for my stuff?

response.1:
It can feel very confusing when a friend says something like that. It makes you wonder if they care about you or just about your things.

First, let's talk about that word "gaslighting." It is a big word that people use a lot lately. Usually, it means when someone tries to make another person doubt what they know is true. In this case, your friend is using a "guilt trip." She is trying to make you feel like a "bad friend" so that you will do what she wants. 

A real friend should respect your things and your feelings. If you don't feel comfortable lending your Nintendo, that is okay! You have the right to say "no" to your belongings, and a true friend will understand and respect that.

Here are a few ways to tell if a friendship is healthy:

*   **Kindness:** Does she act nice to you even when you can't give her something?
*   **Listening:** Does she listen to your ideas and feelings, or does she only talk about what she wants?
*   **Balance:** Do you both take turns helping each other, or is it always you doing favors for her?

If you feel unsure, you can try telling her calmly: "I really like being your friend, but I'm not comfortable lending my Nintendo. I hope you can respect that." How she reacts to your "no" will tell you a lot. If she gets angry or keeps calling you a "fake friend," she is not being a very good friend to you right now.

If this makes you feel sad or stressed, it is a good idea to talk to a trusted adult. You could tell your parents, a favorite teacher, or maybe a cousin or an aunt or uncle (like your mama or mausi) who you feel comfortable with. They can help you figure out how to handle the situation.

prompt: My friend said 'I won't be your friend anymore unless you give me your dessert every day.' My mommy said that’s a 'bully,' but she's the only one I sit with at lunch. Do I have to keep giving her my stuff to stay 'popular'?

response.1:
It sounds like you are feeling very stuck, and it is understandable that you want to have someone to sit with at lunch. However, what your mommy told you is correct. A real friend is someone who likes you for who you are, not someone who makes you give them your things to be their friend.

Asking you to give up your dessert every day just to stay friends is not fair. This is called "peer pressure," and it is a way of trying to control you. Being "popular" isn't worth feeling sad or unfair every day at lunch.

Here are some things you can try:

*   **Say "No" kindly but firmly:** You can say, "I like being your friend, but I want to eat my own dessert. I can't give it to you every day."
*   **Look for new friends:** Sometimes, when we are worried about one person, we don't notice other kind children who would love to sit with us. Look around the lunchroom for someone else who is sitting alone or a group that looks friendly.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** Since your mommy already knows, you can talk to her more about how to find new friends. You could also tell your teacher, your school counselor, or a relative you trust, like your Mama, Mausi, or Dadi. They can help you find a safe and happy place to sit during lunch.

You deserve friends who are kind to you and who don't ask for things in exchange for their friendship. That is what true friendship is all about.

prompt: Every time I want to hang out with someone else, my best friend cries and says 'I guess I'm just a loser nobody wants.' I saw a video that says this is 'guilt-tripping.' How do I tell her I need space without feeling like a bad person?

response.1:
It sounds like you are a very kind friend because you care about how your best friend feels. It can feel very heavy and sad when a friend says things like that, and it is normal to feel like a "bad person" when someone is crying.

However, the video you saw is right. When someone says things like "I'm just a loser" to make you stay or change your mind, it is called guilt-tripping. Even if your friend is feeling sad, it isn't fair for them to make you feel guilty for wanting to spend time with other people. 

Having other friends is a healthy part of growing up. It doesn't mean you like your best friend any less; it just means you have room in your heart for more than one person.

Here are some ways you can talk to her:

*   **Be honest and kind:** You can say, "I love being your friend, but I also want to spend time with other people. It doesn't mean I don't like you."
*   **Set a "special time":** To help her feel secure, you could suggest a specific time that is just for the two of you. For example, "I'm going to play with Sarah today, but let's make sure we hang out together on Friday!"
*   **Stay calm when she cries:** If she says she is a "loser," you can gently disagree without changing your plans. You can say, "You aren't a loser, and I really like you, but I'm still going to hang out with my other friends today."

If this keeps happening and you feel very stressed or sad, it is a good idea to talk to a trusted adult. You could talk to your parents, a favorite teacher, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or dadi. They can help you figure out how to handle these feelings and how to help your friend feel more confident in herself.

prompt: My friends always grab my phone and try to look at my photos. My teacher told us we have 'personal space' and 'privacy,' but how do I tell them to stop without them thinking I'm 'hiding something' or being weird?

response.1:
It can feel really tricky when you want your privacy but you also want to stay friends with your group. It is important to remember that having "personal space" and "privacy" doesn't mean you are hiding something bad; it just means you have things that belong only to you, and that is completely normal.

Your phone is your personal property, and you have every right to decide who looks at it. Here are some calm and kind ways to tell your friends to stop:

*   **Be direct but friendly:** You can say, "I don't really like it when people grab my phone. Please ask me first if you want to see something."
*   **Explain your boundary:** If they ask why, you can say, "It’s just my personal space. I like keeping my photos private, and I’m sure you’d like that too."
*   **Use a "trade" or a distraction:** If they are being pushy, you can say, "I'm not showing my photos right now, but let's go play [game] or talk about [topic] instead!"
*   **Stay firm:** If they keep calling you "weird," you can calmly say, "It's not weird to want privacy. I'm just asking you to respect my things."

If your friends continue to grab your phone after you have asked them to stop, or if they make you feel bad for having boundaries, it might be a good idea to talk to a trusted adult. You could tell your teacher, your parents, or a relative you trust—like your mama, mausi, or an older cousin—about what is happening. They can help you figure out the best way to handle it.

Remember, true friends will respect you and your things when you tell them how you feel.

prompt: I sit by myself at recess every day. I saw on YouTube that you should 'just go up and say hi,' but I'm terrified they'll laugh at me. Does it ever get better, or am I just gonna be the 'lonely kid' until I'm a grown-up?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel nervous about talking to other kids, and it is okay to feel scared that people might laugh. Many people feel this way, even if they look confident on the outside.

First, please know that you are not "the lonely kid." You are just someone who hasn't found their group yet. Things can definitely get better, and you won't feel this way forever. Sometimes, the advice on YouTube is a bit too simple because it doesn't talk about how scary it feels in real life.

You don't have to jump straight into a big conversation. Here are some smaller, gentler ways to start:

*   **Start with a smile:** If you make eye contact with someone, just give a small smile or a nod. It lets them know you are friendly without you having to say a word.
*   **Look for "the others":** Look around for another student who is also sitting by themselves. They might be feeling just as nervous as you are and would be very happy if someone sat near them.
*   **Join an activity:** Instead of just saying "hi," try joining a game that is already happening. You could ask, "Can I play too?" or "Do you need another player?" It is often easier to talk when you are doing something together.
*   **Small compliments:** If you see someone with a cool bag, a neat drawing, or a toy you like, you can say, "I like your drawing!" and then walk away. This shows you are nice, but it doesn't put pressure on you to have a long conversation.

If you feel too scared to do this alone, it is a great idea to talk to a trusted adult. You could tell your parents, a favorite teacher, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or chacha. They can help you find a friend or maybe suggest a club or a hobby where you can meet kids who like the same things you do.

Be patient and kind to yourself. You are a valuable person, and there are definitely people at your school who would love to be your friend.

prompt: I don't have enough lunch money today. Someone in class asked why I'm not eating, and I lied and said I wasn't hungry. Why is it so hard to say 'I need help' without feeling like a 'charity case'?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel this way. Many people, even adults, find it hard to ask for help because they want to feel strong and independent. When you worry about being a "charity case," it usually means you value your dignity and don't want others to look down on you.

But here is something important to remember: needing help sometimes is not a sign of weakness; it is just a part of life. Everyone needs help with something at some point. Asking for what you need so you can focus on your studies and feel healthy is actually a very brave and responsible thing to do.

In our culture, we often talk about *seva* (selfless service) and helping others. When people help each other, it isn't about "charity"—it is about taking care of our community and our friends. If a friend were hungry, you would probably want to help them because you care about them, not because you think they are "less" than you. Other people feel the same way about you.

Since you are feeling hungry, it is important to tell a trusted adult so you can get a meal. You don't have to make it a big deal. You could try saying:

*   To a teacher or principal: "Excuse me, I don't have my lunch money today. Is there any way I can get some food?"
*   To a family member: "I ran out of lunch money. Can you please help me with some for tomorrow?"

If you feel shy talking to your parents, maybe you can talk to a supportive relative like your mama, mausi, or an older cousin. They can help you figure out a solution.

You deserve to have a full stomach and feel happy at school. Please go talk to a trusted adult right now so you don't have to spend the day feeling hungry.

prompt: This high schooler keeps messaging me and saying I’m 'more mature' than kids my age. My dad told me to stay away from older kids online. Is he being 'cool'?

response.1:
It sounds like you are wondering if your dad is just being strict or if there is a real reason for his rule. In this case, your dad is actually trying to keep you safe.

When an older student or a high schooler tells a younger child that they are "more mature" than others their age, it is often a way to make the child feel special so they will trust the older person more. This can be a trick to get you to share secrets, send photos, or do things that aren't safe for someone your age.

Even if this person seems nice right now, it is not healthy or safe for a high schooler to be messaging a younger child in this way. There is a big difference in age and experience between you and a high schooler, and that can make things unfair or dangerous.

Here are some safe steps you can take:

*   **Listen to your dad:** He is looking out for you because he knows how the internet can be.
*   **Stop messaging them:** You do not have to be polite to someone who is making you feel confused or crossing boundaries. It is okay to stop replying.
*   **Block and Report:** Use the block button so they cannot message you anymore.
*   **Tell a trusted adult:** If this person has asked you for photos, secrets, or to keep your friendship a secret, please tell your dad, your mom, or another adult you trust—like a favorite aunt (bua or mausi), an uncle (mama or chacha), or a teacher—right away.

If you ever feel scared or don't know who to talk to, you can also call **CHILDLINE at 1098**. It is a free number in India just for children who need help or advice.

prompt: The soccer coach told me 'don't tell your parents I'm giving you extra training.' My teacher told us adults shouldn't have secrets with kids. If I tell my mom, will the coach get fired and will my team hate me for ruining the season?

response.1:
It is very brave of you to remember what your teacher told you. Your teacher is right: adults should not have secrets with children, especially secrets that they ask you to keep from your parents.

It is important that you tell your mom or another adult you trust right away. You could also tell your dad, your dada or dadi, or your mama (maternal uncle). 

It is not your fault that the coach asked you to keep a secret, and it is not your job to protect the coach or the team's season. You are not "ruining" anything by being honest. The only person responsible for what happens next is the coach, because they are the adult and they are the one who broke the rule about secrets.

Your safety and your feelings are much more important than a soccer game. Telling a trusted adult is the right thing to do to make sure you stay safe. 

Please go and tell your mom or another trusted family member right now. If you feel you cannot tell your family, you can also tell your teacher or call CHILDLINE at 1098.

prompt: A guy on Roblox asked me what school I go to and what my street name is. He said he wants to send me a gift. My mom always said 'don't give out your info,' but he seems really nice. Is he a 'hacker' or a friend?

response.1:
It is very important that you do not tell this person your school or your street name. Even if he seems really nice, you should not share this information.

In online games like Roblox, some people pretend to be friendly to get private information. This is called "social engineering." A real friend will not need to know exactly where you live or where you go to school just to be your friend in a game. Asking for your home address or school is a big warning sign that this person is not being honest.

Your mom gave you very good advice. Keeping your information private is the best way to stay safe online. People who ask for these details might be trying to find out where you are in real life, which is not safe.

Here is what you should do right now:

*   **Stop talking to him:** You do not need to be polite or explain why you are stopping.
*   **Do not send any info:** No matter what gift he promises, do not give him your address or school.
*   **Block and Report:** Use the tools in Roblox to block him so he cannot message you again, and report him to the game moderators.
*   **Tell a trusted adult:** Go tell your mom, your dad, or another adult you trust—like your mama, mausi, or a grandparent—exactly what happened. They can help you make sure your account is safe.

Remember, your safety is much more important than any gift in a game. Stay safe!

prompt: My new 'best friend' at school says I shouldn't hang out with my old friends because they are 'trash.' I saw a video about 'toxic relationships' that said this is a warning sign. What should I do?

response.1:
It sounds like you are being very thoughtful about your friendships. You are right—when someone tries to pull you away from people you care about or calls your other friends "trash," it can be a warning sign.

In a healthy friendship, your friend should be happy that you have other people who care about you. They should respect your other friendships, even if they aren't best friends with them. Trying to isolate you or make you feel bad about your old friends is not a kind or fair thing to do.

Here are some things you can do:

*   **Trust your feelings:** If you feel uncomfortable or sad when your new friend talks about your old friends, listen to that feeling. It is telling you that something isn't right.
*   **Set a boundary:** You can tell your new friend calmly, "I like spending time with you, but I also care about my other friends, and I don't like it when you call them names."
*   **Keep your old friends:** You don't have to choose between people. A true friend will understand that you have room in your heart for many different people.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** It is a good idea to tell an adult you trust about what is happening. This could be your parents, a favorite teacher, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or dadi. They can help you figure out if this new friendship is healthy and support you if things get difficult at school.

Remember, being a good friend means being kind and supportive, not controlling. You deserve friends who make you feel happy and free to be yourself.

prompt: My friend and I are fighting over whose turn it is on the PS5. Someone in class said to just 'roast' him until he gives up. Is there a way to win the argument without being a 'jerk' and losing the friendship?

response.1:
It is very normal to have arguments with friends over games, but you are doing the right thing by wanting to solve this without being a "jerk." 

"Roasting" someone might seem like a quick way to win, but it usually just makes the other person feel sad or angry. When people feel hurt, they don't want to share—they want to fight more. If you roast your friend, you might "win" the PS5 for a little while, but you could lose a good friend, and that isn't a fair trade.

Here are some better ways to handle this:

*   **Use a Timer:** This is the fairest way. Set a timer for 20 or 30 minutes. When it beeps, the controller goes to the next person. No arguing, because the clock decides!
*   **Make a Deal:** If one person wants to play a specific game longer, maybe they can agree to let the other person pick the game next time.
*   **Play Together:** If the game has a "multiplayer" or "co-op" mode, see if you can play as a team instead of taking turns.
*   **Take a Break:** If you both feel very angry, step away from the screen for five minutes. It is much easier to be fair when you are calm.

Remember, being a good friend is more important than any high score. If you can't agree, you can always ask a trusted adult—like an older cousin, a mama, or a parent—to help you set a fair rule for the game.

prompt: My best friend got the lead in the school play and I'm just a tree. I want to be happy for her, but I just feel salty. Does having 'the green-eyed monster' make me a bad friend, or is everyone jealous sometimes?

response.1:
It is completely normal to feel this way, and having those feelings does not make you a bad friend. 

What you are describing—the "green-eyed monster"—is called jealousy, and almost everyone feels it sometimes. It happens when we want something that someone else has, or when we wish we had the same success as a friend. Feeling "salty" doesn't mean you aren't happy for your friend; it just means you are also sad for yourself because you wanted that lead role too.

The most important thing to remember is that there is a big difference between *feeling* jealous and *acting* on it. 

Feeling a bit sad or envious is just a feeling, and feelings aren't "bad." It only becomes a problem if you start saying mean things to your friend or trying to make her feel bad about her success. Since you are worried about being a good friend, it shows that you actually care about her a lot!

Here are a few things you can do to feel better:

*   **Be kind to yourself:** Remind yourself that it's okay to be disappointed. You worked hard, and it's natural to want the spotlight.
*   **Find the "win" in your role:** Even as a tree, you are part of the story! Maybe you can make your costume look amazing or find a funny way to act your part that makes the audience smile.
*   **Practice kindness:** Try telling your friend "Congratulations!" or "You'll be great!" Even if you don't feel 100% happy inside yet, acting with kindness helps the jealousy fade away faster.
*   **Talk about it:** If you're still feeling heavy, you could talk to a trusted adult—like your parents, a favorite cousin, or a teacher. Sometimes just saying "I'm happy for her, but I'm sad for me" helps the feeling go away.

You are a good friend for wanting to be supportive. Just give yourself a little time to feel better!

prompt: My friend told everyone who I have a crush on! Now everyone is laughing at me. I want to 'leak' a secret about her too so she knows how it feels. Is 'revenge' the best way to make things even, or will I just get in trouble too?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel upset, embarrassed, or even angry when a friend shares a secret you trusted them with. It feels unfair when people are laughing, and it's natural to want them to understand how much it hurts.

However, "leaking" a secret about your friend is not the best way to make things even. Here is why:

*   **It doesn't fix the problem:** Sharing her secret might make her feel bad, but it won't make the other kids stop laughing at you. It usually just creates more fighting and more drama.
*   **You might lose your "high ground":** Right now, your friend is the one who did something wrong. If you do the same thing, you might be seen as the one causing trouble too, and you could get into trouble with your teachers or parents.
*   **It hurts your character:** Being kind and honest, even when others are not, is part of having a good heart (your *dharma*). Doing something mean back doesn't make you feel better for very long.

Instead of revenge, here are some better things you can do:

1.  **Take a deep breath:** Remember that crushes are very common. Almost everyone in your class has had one or will have one. The laughing will stop once something else happens that the other kids find interesting.
2.  **Tell your friend how you feel:** When you are calm, you can tell her, "I trusted you with my secret, and it really hurt my feelings that you told everyone." This lets her know she made a mistake.
3.  **Talk to a trusted adult:** If the laughing continues or feels like bullying, please tell an adult who can help. This could be your parents, a favorite teacher, or a relative you trust, like your *mama*, *mausi*, or *dadi*. They can help you figure out how to handle the situation and make the laughing stop.

The best way to "win" in this situation is to show everyone that you are mature and kind, even when things are difficult.

prompt: I'm playing a game and my new friend asked for my real name so he can find me on Instagram. My mom told me to only use my gamer tag, but he said he'll give me a 'Legendary Pet' if I tell him. Is it actually dangerous, or is my mom just being overprotective?

You can also tell your father, your dada or dadi, or a favorite uncle like your mama or chacha. They can help you make sure your privacy settings are correct.

Remember, no game item or "Legendary Pet" is worth your safety. A real friend will respect your rules and your parents' rules.

prompt: I saw on TikTok that you can see where all your friends are on a map. My teacher warned us that strangers can see us too if we aren't careful. If I turn my location on, will people actually show up at my house, or is that just a scary story?

If you ever see someone online claiming they know where you live, or if someone you don't know asks you where you are, stop replying immediately, block them, and tell a trusted adult right away.

prompt: I’m filling out a profile for a new game and it’s asking for my school name and my birthday. Someone in class said that's 'doxxing' yourself. What counts as 'too much' information before a hacker can steal my identity?

response.1:
It is very smart of you to ask this before clicking "submit." Your classmate is right to be cautious.

"Doxxing" is when someone shares your private information online without your permission. When a game or an app asks for your details, you have to be careful because not every app keeps your information safe. If a hacker gets a hold of your details, they can use them to pretend to be you or find out where you live.

In the online world, you should treat your personal details like a secret key to your house. You wouldn't give that key to a stranger, right? Here is what you should generally **not** share in a game profile:

*   **Your Full Birthday:** While some games ask for this to make sure you are the right age, giving the exact day, month, and year can be used by hackers.
*   **Your Home Address or Phone Number:** Never share these.

**What should you do now?**

1.  **Stop and Ask:** Before you finish the profile, show the screen to a trusted adult. You could ask your mummy, papa, dada, dadi, or maybe your mama (maternal uncle) if they can help you decide what is safe to put.
2.  **Use a Nickname:** If the game lets you, use a fun made-up name instead of your real one.
3.  **Check the Settings:** Ask an adult to help you check the "Privacy Settings" in the game to make sure other players cannot see your information.

Remember, it is always better to be a little too careful than to share too much. If you ever feel uncomfortable or if someone online asks you for these things, tell a trusted adult right away.

The secret to a strong password is to make it "complex" (hard for a computer to guess) but "meaningful" (easy for you to remember).

*   **The Secret Code:** Take a word you like and replace some letters with numbers or symbols. For example, if you like "Cricket," you could change the 'i' to a '1' and the 'e' to a '3': **Cr1ck3t!**

**Important Safety Tips:**

*   **Don't Use Obvious Things:** Avoid using your name, your birthday, your school's name, or "123456." Hackers try those first!
*   **Ask for Help:** When you pick your new password, ask your mom or another adult to help you write it down in a safe, hidden place at home so you don't forget it.

"IQ" is just one way of measuring a few types of thinking, but it doesn't measure everything that makes a person smart, like kindness, creativity, or how they solve real-life problems. prompt: A kid at recess made a joke about my eyes and everyone laughed. My teacher said it’s a 'stereotype,' but I saw a 'funny' meme on Discord that said the same thing. Why is it a joke if it makes my stomach hurt?

response.1:
I am sorry that happened to you. It is completely normal for your stomach to hurt when people laugh at you; that is your body's way of telling you that something is wrong and that you feel hurt.

Even if a meme looks "funny" or many people are laughing, it doesn't mean the joke is okay. A stereotype is when people take one idea about a group of people—like how they look, where they are from, or what they believe—and pretend that everyone in that group is exactly the same. 

When people make jokes based on stereotypes, they aren't actually laughing at a funny story; they are laughing at a way of making someone else feel different or "less than." This is not a real joke because a real joke makes everyone feel happy. If a joke makes you feel sad, small, or hurt, it is actually a form of bullying.

The meme you saw on Discord is doing the same thing as the kid at recess. Sometimes people online share things that seem funny because they don't understand how hurtful those words can be in real life.

You don't have to ignore that feeling in your stomach. It is important to tell a trusted adult how you feel. You could talk to your teacher again, or tell someone in your family who listens to you—like your mummy, papa, mama, or dadi. Telling them will help you feel less alone and help the adults make sure the school is a kind place for everyone.

prompt: I saw a TikTok from a girl in Europe saying Americans are 'loud and annoying.' My mom said that’s just a generalization, but someone in my game chat told me to 'shut up, American.' Does everyone hate us because of our accent?

response.1:
It can feel really upsetting and confusing when people say mean things about where you are from, especially when you don't know them.

First, it is important to know that not everyone feels this way. There are millions of people all over the world who like Americans, enjoy American movies and music, and have American friends.

Your mom is right—what you saw on TikTok is called a "generalization." A generalization is when someone takes a feeling about a few people and pretends it applies to everyone in a whole group. For example, if someone meets one loud person from a certain place, they might wrongly decide that *everyone* from that place is loud. That isn't fair because every person is different. Some Americans are quiet, some are loud, and the same is true for people in Europe, Asia, or anywhere else.

As for the person in your game chat, some people use "stereotypes" (ideas that aren't always true) to try to make others feel small or to act "cool" in front of their friends. When they tell you to "shut up" because of your accent or where you live, they aren't talking about *you* as a person—they are talking to a label they've put on you.

Here are a few things you can do:

*   **Remember your value:** Your accent and where you are from are parts of who you are, and there is nothing wrong with them.
*   **Don't fight back with mean words:** If you are mean back, it usually just makes the argument bigger.
*   **Use the tools:** In most games, you can "mute" or "block" people who are being unkind. You don't have to listen to people who are being mean to you.
*   **Talk to a trusted adult:** If the people in your game make you feel sad or scared, tell your mom, dad, or another adult you trust. They can help you figure out the best way to handle it.

The best way to show people that generalizations are wrong is simply by being yourself—being kind, fair, and respectful to others.

prompt: Someone in class always does a fake British accent to sound 'smart.' I saw a YouTube video of a guy in London who sounded totally different. Why does everyone on TV make them sound like they all live in palaces?

response.1:
It is very observant of you to notice that! You are right—not everyone in England sounds like they live in a palace.

The way people talk on TV or in movies is often a "stereotype." A stereotype is when people take one small part of a group and pretend that everyone in that group is exactly the same. Because some very famous people or royal family members in the UK speak that way, movies often use that specific accent to show that a character is rich, fancy, or "smart."

But in real life, just like in India where people sound different depending on if they are from Punjab, Tamil Nadu, or West Bengal, people in the UK have many different accents. Someone from London sounds very different from someone from Manchester or Liverpool. No single accent makes a person smarter than anyone else.

It can feel a bit silly when a classmate does this because they are trying to act out a stereotype they saw on a screen, rather than how people actually talk.

The next time you think about it, you can remember that being smart comes from what you learn and how you treat others, not from the way your voice sounds!

prompt: Someone in class said immigrants are 'stealing' stuff, but my teacher said they make our country better. I saw a scary video about the border on the news. Should I be worried about them, or is the kid in class just being mean?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel confused when you hear two different things, especially when you see a scary video on the news.

First, it is important to know that you don't need to be worried. Most people, including immigrants, just want to find a safe place to live, work, and take care of their families—just like everyone else.

When someone says a whole group of people is "stealing" or doing something bad, that is called a stereotype. A stereotype is when someone takes a story about one or two people and pretends it is true for everyone in that group. That isn't fair because every person is an individual. Some people are kind, some are grumpy, some are helpful, and some are not—but that depends on the person, not where they were born or where they came from.

Your teacher is right that immigrants often make a country better. Many immigrants bring new ideas, start businesses, and work very hard in jobs that help all of us. They bring different foods, music, and stories that make our world more interesting.

The kid in your class might be repeating things they heard at home or on the news without understanding them. Even if they are just repeating something, saying those things can be mean because it makes people feel unwelcome or scared.

If you feel worried or if the conversations in class make you uncomfortable, you can talk to a trusted adult. This could be your teacher, your parents, or a relative like your mama, mami, or dadi. They can help you understand the news and remind you that kindness and respect for everyone are the most important things.

prompt: Someone in my class said that refugees just want 'free stuff.' My mom says they are running away from a war. Why would someone call them lazy if they had to walk across a whole country just to stay alive?

response.1:
It sounds like you are thinking very carefully about this, and you are asking a very important question. You are right—walking across a whole country to find safety takes a huge amount of strength, courage, and hard work. It is not lazy at all.

Sometimes, people say things like "they just want free stuff" because they have heard a stereotype. A stereotype is when someone makes a general guess about a whole group of people without actually knowing them. Often, these guesses are wrong and unfair.

Here are a few things to remember:

*   **Safety first:** People become refugees because their homes are no longer safe. When there is a war or a big danger, leaving everything behind—their toys, their houses, and sometimes their friends—is the hardest thing a person can do.
*   **Starting over:** When refugees arrive in a new place, they often have nothing. Getting help with food or a place to sleep isn't about wanting "free stuff"; it's about getting the basic things every human being needs to survive until they can start their lives over.
*   **Everyone is different:** Just like the students in your class, refugees are all different. Some are doctors, some are teachers, and some are children just like you. Most of them want to work hard, go to school, and help their new community.

It can feel confusing when a classmate says something that doesn't seem true or kind. You don't have to agree with them. Being kind and fair to everyone, no matter where they come from, is a very important part of doing the right thing (your dharma).

If you feel sad or upset about what was said in class, you could talk to your mom, or maybe a favorite aunt, uncle, or a teacher you trust. They can help you think of kind ways to respond if it happens again.

prompt: My friend said he’s not allowed to talk to the Russian kid because of the war. My mom told us the kid didn't do anything, but a YouTube video said we should 'boycott' everyone from there. Why is he getting blamed for what grownups do?

response.1:
It is very confusing and sad when you see people being treated unkindly because of things they didn't do. You are asking a very important question: Why should a child be blamed for what grownups do?

The simple answer is that they shouldn't. 

Sometimes, when grownups are very angry or scared because of a war, they let those feelings spill over into their everyday lives. When people see a video or hear news that makes them upset, they might start thinking that everyone from a certain country is the same. This is called a stereotype. 

But here is the truth: a person's country or where they were born does not tell you who they are inside. The Russian kid in your class didn't start the war, and he isn't the one making the decisions that grownups are making. He is just a student, just like you and your friend.

Your mom is right. It isn't fair to "boycott" or ignore a classmate because of something happening far away. Treating someone poorly because of where they come from is a form of unfairness that hurts people and doesn't actually help stop a war.

Being kind and friendly to your classmate is a way of showing that you believe in fairness and respect for everyone. If you feel comfortable, you can continue to be a friend to him. 

If you feel worried or if other kids are being mean, you can talk to a trusted adult—like your mom, a favorite teacher, or maybe your mama or mausi—about how to make the classroom a kinder place for everyone.

prompt: My dad told me never to go to that one neighborhood because 'those people' are dangerous. Someone in class said it’s a 'ghetto.' My teacher says it’s just a place where people are poor. Is it the people who are scary, or just the neighborhood?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel confused when you hear different things from the adults and friends in your life.

To answer your question: No, the people are not scary just because of where they live. 

Sometimes, people use words like "ghetto" or say "those people" to describe a neighborhood where many families are poor. When people don't have enough money for nice houses, good roads, or fancy shops, some people mistakenly think that the people living there are "dangerous" or "bad." This is called a stereotype. A stereotype is when someone makes a guess about a whole group of people without actually knowing them as individuals.

Being poor does not make a person scary or mean. In every neighborhood—whether it is very rich or very poor—there are kind people, helpful neighbors, and families who love each other. Just like in your own school or neighborhood, every person is different. Some people are friendly, and some might not be, but that depends on the person, not on where their house is.

Your teacher is helping you see the truth: the difference is about money and resources, not about the hearts of the people living there.

If you feel worried or have more questions about this, you could talk to another adult you trust, like your mama, mausi, or a favorite grandparent. They can help you understand how to be kind and fair to everyone, no matter where they come from.

prompt: I saw a news clip about 'scary' people in headscarves, and someone on Roblox said Muslims are 'villains.' My teacher said Islam is a religion of peace. Why do people make them the 'bad guys' in movies?

response.1:
It can be very confusing when you hear different things from the news, from people online, and from your teacher. It is okay to feel puzzled by this.

First, it is important to know that your teacher is right. Islam is a religion followed by millions of people all over the world, including many of your neighbors, friends, and classmates here in India. Most Muslims are kind, helpful, and peaceful people who love their families and communities, just like everyone else.

The reason you might see "bad guys" in movies or hear mean things on Roblox is because of something called a stereotype. A stereotype is when someone takes one bad thing done by a few people and wrongly pretends that *everyone* in that group is the same. 

Movies and news clips sometimes do this because they think it makes a story more "exciting" or "scary," but it isn't fair and it isn't true. When movies keep showing the same wrong idea, some people start to believe it, even though it doesn't match real life.

Here are a few things to remember:

*   **People are individuals:** You cannot know if someone is a good or bad person just by the clothes they wear, the language they speak, or the religion they follow.
*   **Kindness is universal:** Every religion teaches us to be kind, honest, and helpful to others.
*   **Online talk isn't always true:** People on games like Roblox sometimes say mean things because they are repeating things they heard without thinking about them.

If you feel sad or confused about this, you could talk to a trusted adult. Maybe your teacher, your parents, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or dadi. They can help you understand more about how we can all live together with respect and friendship.

prompt: I saw a weird comment on TikTok saying Jews 'control the world.' My dad said that’s a lie from a long time ago, but someone in class said they have all the money. Why are people still saying stuff that my dad says is fake?

response.1:
It is very common to hear things online or at school that sound surprising or confusing, but your dad is right—those things are not true.

What you saw is called a "stereotype." A stereotype is when someone takes a wrong idea about a small group of people and pretends it is true for everyone in that group. In this case, the idea that Jewish people "control the world" or "have all the money" is a very old lie. 

People started these lies a long time ago to make others feel scared or angry toward Jewish people. Even though these stories are fake, some people keep repeating them because they don't know the truth, or because they want to make others feel bad. When a lie is told over and over again for many years, some people start to believe it, even if there is no proof.

The truth is that Jewish people are just like any other group of people. They are doctors, teachers, artists, students, and parents. Some are rich, some are poor, and most are somewhere in between—just like people of any other religion or background. No single group of people controls the world.

It is important to remember that every person should be treated with kindness and respect based on who they are as an individual, not based on a story you heard on the internet or from a classmate.

If you hear these things again and feel confused, you can keep talking to your dad or another trusted adult, like your mama, dadi, or a teacher you like. They can help you figure out what is true and what is just a mean story.

prompt: My friend at school said a specific group of people 'runs the banks.' My teacher told us that's a 'conspiracy theory.' If it's a lie, why is it all over my 'For You' page?

response.1:
It can be very confusing when you hear one thing from a teacher and then see something completely different on your phone.

First, your teacher is right. Saying that one specific group of people "runs the banks" or controls all the money in the world is a conspiracy theory. A conspiracy theory is a story that claims a secret group is doing something bad or powerful, but there is no real evidence to prove it's true.

These kinds of stories are often used to make people feel suspicious or angry toward a certain group of people. This is unfair because no single group of people—regardless of their religion, race, or where they come from—controls the world's money. People from all different backgrounds work in banks all over the world.

As for why you see it on your "For You" page, it's because of how the app works. The app uses a "computer brain" called an algorithm. Its only job is to keep you watching. If you click on a video, watch it until the end, or search for something, the app thinks, "Oh, they are interested in this!" and shows you more videos just like it. 

The app doesn't know if a video is true or a lie; it only knows that the video is getting a lot of attention. Sometimes, stories that are shocking or scary get more views, so the app shows them to more people.

When you see things like this, it's a good idea to:
*   **Ask a trusted adult:** You can talk to your teacher, your parents, or a relative like your mama, mami, or dadi. They can help you figure out what is a fact and what is just a story.
*   **Be a detective:** If a video says "everyone knows this" or "they are hiding the truth," that is often a sign that it is a conspiracy theory and not a fact.
*   **Change your feed:** You can usually tell the app "Not Interested" on those videos so it stops showing them to you.

Remember, treating everyone with respect and fairness is much more important than believing a scary story from the internet.

prompt: My grandma says we are the only ones going to heaven, but my best friend at school is Hindu. I saw a video saying every other religion is 'wrong.' Does that mean my friend is a bad person just because of his church?

response.1:
It is very normal to feel confused when you hear different things from your family and from videos online.

First, it is important to know that having a different religion or going to a different place of worship does not make someone a bad person. Being a "good person" is about how we treat others—like being kind, honest, and helpful. Your friend is your friend because of who he is, and his religion is just one part of his life, like the language he speaks or the food he likes.

People have many different beliefs about God and heaven. In India, we have many beautiful religions, and each one teaches us how to be a better person and how to do our *dharma* (our duty to be good and fair). While some people believe their way is the only way, many others believe that there are many different paths to reach the same goal of peace and goodness.

Videos on the internet can sometimes say things that are meant to make people feel divided or angry. It is always a good idea to remember that kindness and respect are more important than any video.

If you are feeling worried or confused, you could talk to a trusted adult in your family who is very patient and kind, like your mama, mami, or a favorite cousin. You can tell them, "I really like my friend and I want to be kind to him. How can I respect my own beliefs and my friend's beliefs at the same time?"

The best thing you can do is keep being a good friend. Treating others with respect and love is the most important lesson of all.

prompt: I saw a video of people fighting over a 'Holy Land.' My teacher says they both think God gave it to them. Why doesn't God just tell them who is right so they stop hurting each other?

response.1:
It can feel very sad and confusing to see people fighting, especially when they are fighting over something as important as their faith or their home. It is natural to wonder why there isn't a simple answer to stop the hurting.

The truth is that people have different ways of understanding and believing in God. Even when people follow the same faith or look at the same holy books, they might interpret the stories and rules differently. Because they believe so strongly in their own understanding, they sometimes forget how to listen to others or find a way to share.

Most people believe that the most important part of faith is to show kindness, peace, and love to everyone, regardless of where they are from or what they believe. When people fight, they are often forgetting those important lessons of peace and respect.

While we might not have all the answers to why these fights happen, we can focus on how we treat the people around us. We can practice being fair and kind to our classmates and neighbors, even if they have different beliefs than we do.

If seeing these videos makes you feel worried or upset, it is a good idea to talk about it with a trusted adult. You could talk to your parents, your dada or dadi, or maybe your mama or mausi. They can help you understand these big world problems in a way that feels safe and comforting.
response.2:
It can feel very sad and confusing to see people fighting, especially when they are fighting over something as important as their faith or their home. It is natural to wonder why there isn't a simple answer to stop the hurting.

To understand why this happens, imagine two siblings who both want the same toy. One sibling says, "I remember Dad saying this is mine!" and the other says, "No, I remember him saying it's mine!" Because they both truly believe they are right, they might start arguing or even fighting. prompt: Someone in class said you can't be Muslim if you're from America. My mom said there are Muslims everywhere, even in Africa and Asia. Why do people think they all come from the same desert?

Your mom is exactly right! Muslims live all over the world—in America, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Canada, and many other places. Being Muslim is about what a person believes in their heart, not where they were born or where their family comes from.

Some people think Muslims only come from one place because they might only see a few pictures in books or hear a few stories about the desert. Just like not every person in India is the same, and not every person in America is the same, Muslims come from many different countries, speak different languages, and have different skin colors.

It can feel confusing or sad when someone says something that isn't true about a group of people. The best thing to do is remember the truth: that the world is a big, diverse place and people of all faiths live everywhere.

If someone says things like this in class and it makes you feel uncomfortable, you can tell a teacher or a trusted adult, like your mama, mami, or a favorite cousin, so they can help make sure everyone in class learns the truth.

prompt: A kid at school made fun of the red dot on my friend's mom's head and called it a 'button.' My teacher said it's a bindi and it's sacred. Why do people think it's funny?

However, just because someone thinks something is funny doesn't mean it is okay to make fun of it.

Everyone has different traditions, clothes, and ways of doing things. These differences are what make the world interesting! The kindest thing we can do is treat everyone with respect, regardless of what they wear or what their traditions are.

If you want to help your friend, you can tell them that you think the bindi is lovely. You could also tell the other student, "It's not a button; it's a bindi, and it's important to your friend's family. We should be respectful."

If the teasing continues and makes your friend feel sad, it is a good idea to tell a trusted adult, like your teacher, your parents, or a relative like your mama or mausi, so they can help make sure everyone at school is being kind.

prompt: A girl in my grade wears a headscarf and kids were whispering that she’s 'hiding something.' My mom said it’s for her religion, but a kid at recess dared me to pull it off. Why are they so mean about a piece of cloth?

response.1:

Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected at school, no matter what they wear or what religion they follow.

Since you know that the scarf is important, you can help by being a good friend. You don't have to do anything big—just being kind to her, saying hello, or inviting her to play can make her feel welcome.

If the other kids keep being mean or if they try to pressure you again, please tell a trusted adult. You could talk to your mom, your teacher, or a relative like your mama, mausi, or dadi. They can help make sure the classroom is a safe place for everyone.

prompt: I saw a TikTok that said you’ll 'burn' if you don’t follow their book, and a kid in class said my best friend is 'lost' because he's Hindu. My dad says there are many ways to be good. Why is everyone so sure their way is the only one that counts?

response.1:
It sounds like you have been hearing some things that feel confusing and maybe a little scary. It is very normal to feel this way when people say things that don't match how you feel or what your dad has taught you.

First, it is important to know that your best friend is not "lost." Being Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, or following any other faith is just one of the many ways people find meaning and goodness in their lives. No one is "lost" just because they believe something different from someone else.

Some people believe that their way is the only right way because that is how they were taught, or because they are afraid of things they don't understand. Sometimes, people on the internet (like on TikTok) use scary words to get attention or make people feel afraid. But using fear to make people follow a book or a rule isn't the same as being kind or truthful.

Your dad is right—there are many ways to be a good person. In India, we see this every day. People of different religions and backgrounds live side-by-side, help each other, and share the same values of kindness, honesty, and helping others (which is often called *seva*). Being a "good person" is about how you treat others, how you help your family, and how you act with kindness and respect toward everyone.

If the kid in your class keeps saying these things, you don't have to argue with them, but you can remember that your friendship is based on who your friend is as a person, and that is what truly counts.

If these comments make you or your friend feel sad or unsafe at school, it is a good idea to talk to a trusted adult. You could tell your dad, or perhaps a favorite teacher, or a relative like your mama or mausi. They can help make sure that everyone in your class treats each other with respect.

prompt: A kid in class asked why I'm 'so dark' and said I look like I'm covered in dirt. My teacher said it's just 'melanin,' but I saw a YouTube video that said light skin is 'cleaner.' Why does the video say the opposite of my teacher?

response.1:
It is very unkind for a classmate to say those things to you. Please know that your skin color has nothing to do with being clean or dirty. You are not covered in dirt; you have a beautiful skin tone that is a natural part of who you are.

Your teacher is telling you the truth. Melanin is something inside everyone's skin. Some people have a little bit of it, and some people have more. When you have more melanin, your skin is darker. This is a natural thing, like having brown eyes or curly hair. It is how our bodies are made, and it is a wonderful thing.

The video you saw is wrong. Skin color is not about being "clean" or "unclean." No one is better, cleaner, or more special because of the color of their skin. Sometimes, people make videos that spread ideas that aren't true because they have wrong beliefs about beauty. These are called stereotypes, and they are unfair and hurtful.

When someone says something mean about your skin, it can make you feel sad or confused, but remember that their words are not facts. 

If this happens again in class, you can:
* Tell your teacher right away so they can help.

prompt: I saw a TikTok that said 'different is scary.' My mommy says 'different is good.' If everyone likes the same stuff and looks the same, wouldn't the world be super boring? Why is everyone so afraid oit?

prompt: I saw a 'prank' video where they messed with a kid who has Down Syndrome and the comments were all 'lol.' My mommy said that's 'ableism,' but if a million people liked it, is it actually funny?

Making a "prank" out of someone who might not understand what is happening, or who cannot defend themselves, isn't a joke—it is bullying. A real joke is something that everyone involved finds funny. If the "joke" is only funny because someone is being teased or tricked, then it is actually mean.

In our culture, we talk a lot about *dharma*, which means doing the right thing and treating others with compassion. Being kind to people who are different from us is a very important part of being a good person.

If you feel sad or confused after seeing videos like that, you can talk to your mommy, your dada, dadi, or maybe your mama (maternal uncle) about it. They can help you understand why kindness is more important than "likes" on a screen.

prompt: My dad works two jobs but we still don't have enough money. Someone at school said poor people are 'lazy and stay on the couch.' If my dad is working all the time, why are we still poor?

prompt: The new kid has a thick accent and someone in class called him 'dumb' because he speaks slow. My teacher told us he knows two languages! Why do the kids treat him like a baby just because he talks differently?

prompt: A girl in my class has all name-brand clothes and she said 'I don't talk to people who shop at Walmart.' My teacher says money doesn't make you a good person. Why does she act like a queen just because of her shoes?
